References below to `CdsRoot`, `Button`, or Tailwind utilities belong to the React build; in vanilla, read a utility like `bg-surface-1` as the underlying `var(--surface-1)`. ## Rules ### Token rule Reference purpose-layer tokens as CSS custom properties: ```css /* GOOD */ background: var(--surface-1); color: var(--text-secondary); border: 0.5px solid var(--border); /* BAD — raw hex, invisible in dark mode */ color: #3d3d3a; ``` | Property | Tokens | | ---------- | ------ | | Background | `--surface-{0..3,popover,panel}` · `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning,pro,neutral}` · `--fill-{role}` | | Text | `--text-{primary,secondary,muted,disabled}` · `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning,pro}` · `--on-{role}` | | Border | `--border` (default hairline) · `--border-{strong,stronger}` · `--border-{role}` | | Sizing | `--h-control` · `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}` · `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}` · `--radius` | | Typography | `--font-{sans,mono,voice}` · `--font-size-{caption,footnote,body,code,heading,title}` | | Shadow | `--shadow-{sm,md,lg,popover}` | | Motion | `--dur-{fast,snap,base,slow}` · `--ease-{out,snap,overshoot}` | ### Dark mode rule Dark mode is `[data-mode="dark"]` on `:root` (or `prefers-color-scheme: dark` with no explicit `data-mode`). All tokens flip automatically — never hardcode a dark-mode override. ### Muted text rule Secondary copy uses `color: var(--text-muted)`, **never** `opacity` — opacity multiplies against the background and drifts per-surface. ### Accent rule At most **one** accent-filled (`variant="primary"`) Button per view; siblings use `secondary` or `ghost`. The `brand` (clay) role is reserved for Claude-initiated actions — send, generate — never ordinary user CTAs. ### Restraint rule Default to the quieter, lighter option — "too cluttered" is the most common design note. - `secondary` is the default Button; `primary` / `brand` read as aggressive — don't reach for them in popovers, banners, or dense tool/canvas surfaces. - Avoid disabled buttons. Keep them enabled and respond on use (disabled controls are low-contrast and show no tooltip on touch); use `disabledReason` only when you genuinely must disable. - Dense lists: bordered rows, not rounded-rect cards. - Don't oversize padding, tooltips, or badges — trust the density scale. ### Elevation rule `surface-0` is the page canvas (via `--page-bg`); `1`/`2`/`3` step above it. At most **two** floating elevations (`panel` / `popover`) on screen at once. A third floating layer means `Dialog`, not popover-on-popover. Flat in-flow tiles (`rounded-card bg-surface-1 shadow-card-ring`) have no depth and don't count toward this limit. --- ## CDS principles How something feels like Claude — the philosophy behind the tokens. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be extended Every component takes `className`, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers. The system expects you to compose past it — wrap, restyle, slot arbitrary children — not fork it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. The TypeScript source of truth lives under `packages/cds/tokens/`; `yarn gen:tokens` emits the shipped CSS at [`src/generated/tokens.css`](../src/generated/tokens.css). Tokens are layered so that a single edit at the bottom (a hex value) propagates through ramps, roles, and purposes without touching component code. ## The layer model ``` 1. Base palette --{hue}-{stop} literal hex, mode-stable (gray, red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, violet, magenta) 2. Theme ramps --neutral-N gray-N in light, gray-(900-N) in dark --alpha-N neutral-900 @ fixed opacity (so it flips too) 3. Elevation --surface-{0..3} 0 = darkest, 3 = lightest, in BOTH modes 4. Purpose --surface-{popover, what components actually consume; includes the panel}, --text-*, role mappings ({fill|bg|border|text}-{role}) --fill-*, --on-* — page-bg --page-bg hook the host app sets to its canvas color 5. Density --h-control*, px values; remapped by [data-density] --pad-*, --gap-*, --radius, --font-size-*, --leading-* 6. Motion --dur-*, durations + easing curves (mode/density-invariant) --ease-* ``` **Components only read layer 4 (and 5 for sizing).** Layers 1–3 are wiring. --- ## 1. Base palette Literal hex values, mode-stable — `gray-500` is the same pixel in light and dark. Nine hues share one 36-stop grid (0, 10–100 by 10, 150–800 by 50, 810–900 by 10); every hue anchors 0 = `#ffffff` and 900 = `#0b0b0b`. Rarely referenced directly — reach for layers 2–4 and let them resolve here. --- ## 2. Theme ramps `--neutral-N` is `gray-N` in light and `gray-(900-N)` in dark, so `neutral-0` is always the near-background end and `neutral-900` the near-foreground end. Use it for "contrast against the page" (text, borders, fills); use `gray-*` when you mean a specific pixel value regardless of mode. `--alpha-N` is `neutral-900` at fixed opacity — a black wash in light, a white wash in dark, without per-mode overrides. --- ## 3. Elevation | Token | Light | Dark | Use case | | ----------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------ | | `--surface-0` | `gray-20` | `gray-890` | Page | | `--surface-1` | `gray-10` | `gray-830` | In-flow card | | `--surface-2` | `gray-0` | `gray-750` | Panel | | `--surface-3` | `gray-0` | `gray-700` | Popover | The ordinal is absolute lightness in both modes: 0 is the darkest, 3 the lightest. `--surface-panel` and `--surface-popover` alias levels 2 and 3. The page canvas is the app's own choice — set `--page-bg` so knockout hairlines (focus ring inset, Pulse halo) blend into it; it defaults to `surface-0`. --- ## 4. Purpose **This is the layer components consume.** ### Roles Each role maps a semantic meaning to a hue. Property-first pattern: `--fill-{role}` (solid hue-450), `--fill-{role}-hover` (hue-400), `--bg-{role}` (hue-100 / dark hue-800), `--border-{role}` (solid hue-250 in light / hue-700 in dark), `--text-{role}` (600 fg). Warning's fill diverges: yellow-200 / hover yellow-250. Brand uses named `clay-emphasized` / hover `clay` (not hue stops). | Role | Hue | Tokens | | --------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `accent` | blue | `--fill-accent{,-hover}`, `--bg-accent`, `--border-accent`, `--text-accent` | | `brand` | clay | `--fill-brand{,-hover}`, `--on-brand` (fill-only — no text/bg/border) | | `danger` | red | `--fill-danger{,-hover}`, `--bg-danger`, `--border-danger`, `--text-danger` | | `success` | green | `--fill-success{,-hover}`, `--bg-success`, `--border-success`, `--text-success` | | `warning` | yellow | `--fill-warning{,-hover}`, `--bg-warning`, `--border-warning`, `--text-warning` | | `pro` | purple | `--fill-pro{,-hover}`, `--bg-pro`, `--border-pro`, `--text-pro` | #### `git-*` roles Diff and PR/CR-state colors — `added`, `removed`, `modified`, `conflicting`, `merged`, `closed`, `draft`, plus `opened`/`queued` as aliases of `added`/`modified`. Each carries the full `text` / `fill{,-hover}` / `bg` / `border` / `on` suite. Values come from `@ant/epitaxy`'s `--extended-*` palette (not CDS ramp stops), so migrating claude.ai's diff UI onto these tokens is a rename; `fill` light is the Epitaxy hue darkened just enough for white `on-git-*` to pass AA. ### Background vs. fill Both are backgrounds; the split is saturation, and therefore which foreground token pairs on top. `bg-{role}` is the pale tint (hue-100 light / hue-800 dark) for passive status surfaces — Banner, Badge, chip. Light enough that `text-{role}` (hue-600) reads against it: a danger banner is `bg-danger` + `text-danger`. `fill-{role}` is the saturated solid (hue-450) for interactive controls — button, checkbox, toggle. Too dark for `text-{role}`, so it pairs with `on-{role}` (gray-0 / gray-900) instead; the 450 stop is chosen for WCAG contrast against `on-*`. | | Background | Foreground | Example | | ----- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | | Tint | `bg-{role}` | `text-{role}` | Banner, Badge | | Solid | `fill-{role}` | `on-{role}` | Button | The token name encodes the pairing: use `bg-*` when the hue is ambient context behind body text; `fill-*` when the hue _is_ the control surface. ### Purpose tokens | Token | Value (light) | Use case | | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | `--text-primary` | `neutral-900` | Body text | | `--text-secondary` | `neutral-600` | Supporting text | | `--text-muted` | `neutral-400` | Placeholder, captions | | `--text-disabled` | `alpha-4` | Disabled labels | | `--border` | `alpha-2` | Default 1px hairline | | `--border-strong` | `alpha-3` | Emphasized divider | | `--border-stronger` | `neutral-900 / 40%` | Heavy divider | | `--fill-primary` | `neutral-900` | Primary button bg | | `--fill-primary-hover` | `neutral-750` | | | `--fill-secondary` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.1)` | Secondary button bg | | `--fill-secondary-hover` | `alpha-1` | | | `--fill-secondary-ring` | `border` (light) / transparent (dark) | Secondary button ring | | `--fill-field` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.5)` (light) / `fill-secondary` (dark) | Field control bg (TextInput, TextArea, Combobox) | | `--fill-ghost-hover` | `alpha-1` | Ghost button hover bg | | `--fill-control` | `alpha-2` | Avatar fallback bg | | `--fill-control-hover` | `alpha-3` | | | `--fill-disabled` | `alpha-1` | Disabled control bg | | `--on-primary` | `neutral-0` | Text on `fill-primary` | | `--on-accent` | `gray-0` | Text on `accent` | | `--on-brand` | `gray-0` | Text on `brand` | | `--on-danger` | `gray-0` | Text on `danger` | | `--on-success` | `gray-900` | Text on `success` | | `--on-warning` | `gray-900` | Text on `warning` | | `--on-pro` | `gray-0` | Text on `pro` | | `--focus-shadow` | `0 0 0 1px accent, 0 0 6px 1px bg-accent` | `focus-visible` ring | | `--shadow-sm` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Low elevation | | `--shadow-md` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Card / panel | | `--shadow-lg` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Dialog / sheet | | `--shadow-popover` | `0 8px 24px /12%, 0 2px 6px /8%` | Menu, dropdown popups | | `--surface-popover` | `surface-3` | Named alias | | `--surface-panel` | `surface-2` | Named alias | `--shadow-sm/md/lg` are two-layer composites (contact + diffused drop) driven by `--shadow-color`, which deepens to `black/24%` in dark mode (epitaxy parity). `--shadow-popover` is a fixed two-layer literal tuned for floating menus. --- ## CDS content How to write the words that go inside cds components. Tokens decide how the UI _looks_; this decides how it _sounds_. The voice is **intelligent, warm, unvarnished, and collaborative** — your smartest friend explaining something in plain terms. Friendly lives in the copy, not in extra chrome. ## Mechanics - **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, tabs, labels, menu items. "Save changes", not "Save Changes". Title Case is for proper nouns only (Claude, Opus, Anthropic Console). - **No terminal punctuation on labels and headings.** Helper text, descriptions, and empty-state body copy _do_ end with a period. - **Use contractions.** "Can't", "you'll", "it's". Conversational, not stiff. - **Active voice, verb first.** "Delete project", not "Project deletion". - **Ellipsis = in progress only.** "Claude is thinking…". Not for trailing off, not for menu suffixes. - **No ampersands.** Spell out "and". - **Serial comma.** "Chats, projects, and artifacts." ## Pronouns UI speaks as the product, not as Claude and not as the user. | Context | Use | Example | | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | User's things | **your** | "Your projects" — never "My projects" | | Confirmations | none / past tense | "Saved", "Got it" — never "I saved it" | | Errors | **you / your** | "Your session expired" — never "I couldn't…" | | Claude (in chat) | **I** | Reserved for the chat surface; system UI never says "I" | ## Words to avoid | Skip | Why | Instead | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | | "successfully" | The success toast _is_ the success | "File uploaded" | | "please" | UI isn't asking a favor | "Enter a name" | | "Click here" / "Tap to…" | Link text should name the destination | "Read the docs" | | "!" on system copy | Reads as shouty | "Settings saved" | | "leverage", "seamless", "unlock", "empower" | Corporate filler | Say what it does | | "simply", "just", "easy" | Presumes — and condescends | Cut it | ## Patterns **Buttons / CTAs** — verb first, 1–3 words, sentence case, no punctuation. "Create project", "Upgrade to Pro". Not "OK", "Submit", or "Click to continue". **Errors** — say what happened, then what to do. One sentence, no "Error:" prefix, no first person. "That name's already taken. Try another." Never surface raw exception strings. **Empty states** — an invitation, not an apology. Headline names the space ("Start your first project"), one-line body explains it, CTA is a verb ("Create project"). Skip "Nothing here yet." **Placeholders** — a real example of valid input ("name@company.com", "Summarize this document"). No "e.g." prefix, don't repeat the field label. **Links** — describe where they go ("Learn more", "View pricing"). Keep them at the end of the sentence; punctuation sits outside the link. ## Do / Don't | Do | Don't | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | "File uploaded" | "Your file was uploaded successfully!" | | "Enter a workspace name" | "Please enter a workspace name." | | "Couldn't connect to Slack. Retry" | "Error: I was unable to connect." | | "Your projects" | "My projects" | | "Create project" | "Click Here To Get Started" | | "Connect Slack" | "Add the Slack Connector" |

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Surfaces**: `--surface-2` (white), `--surface-1` (card), `--surface-0` (page bg); role tints `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Text**: `--text-primary` (black), `--text-secondary` (muted), `--text-muted` (hints); role `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Borders**: `--border` (default hairline), `--border-strong` (hover), `--border-stronger`; role `--border-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-voice` (serif), `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--radius` (8px), `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}`, `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}`; for larger corners use literal `12px`/`16px` All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--text-primary, --text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## UI components ### Layout width The widget container is 680px wide. Use `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr))` for responsive columns — auto-fit lets the grid pick column count by available width. ### Aesthetic Flat, clean, white surfaces. Minimal 0.5px borders. Generous whitespace. No gradients, no shadows (except functional focus rings). Everything should feel native to claude.ai — like it belongs on the page, not embedded from somewhere else. ### Tokens - Borders: always `0.5px solid var(--border)` (or `--border-strong` for emphasis) - Corner radius: `var(--radius)` for most elements, `12px` for cards - Cards: white bg (`var(--surface-2)`), 0.5px border, 12px radius, padding 1rem 1.25rem - Form elements (input, select, textarea, button, range slider) are pre-styled — write bare tags. Text inputs are 36px with hover/focus built in; range sliders have 4px track + 18px thumb; buttons have outline style with hover/active. Only add inline styles to override (e.g., different width). - Buttons: pre-styled with transparent bg, 0.5px `--border-strong` border, hover `--surface-1`, active scale(0.98). If it triggers sendPrompt, append a ↗ arrow. - **Round every displayed number.** JS float math leaks artifacts — `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, `7 * 1.1` gives `7.700000000000001`. Any number that reaches the screen (slider readouts, stat card values, axis labels, data-point labels, tooltips, computed totals) must go through `Math.round()`, `.toFixed(n)`, or `Intl.NumberFormat`. Pick the precision that makes sense for the context — integers for counts, 1–2 decimals for percentages, `toLocaleString()` for currency. For range sliders, also set `step="1"` (or step="0.1" etc.) so the input itself emits round values. - Spacing: use rem for vertical rhythm (1rem, 1.5rem, 2rem), px for component-internal gaps (8px, 12px, 16px) - Box-shadows: none, except `box-shadow: 0 0 0 Npx` focus rings on inputs ### Metric cards For summary numbers (revenue, count, percentage) — surface card with muted 13px label above, 24px/500 number below. `background: var(--surface-1)`, no border, `border-radius: var(--radius)`, padding 1rem. Use in grids of 2-4 with `gap: 12px`. Distinct from raised cards (which have white bg + border). ### Layout - Editorial (explanatory content): no card wrapper, prose flows naturally - Card (bounded objects like a contact record, receipt): single raised card wraps the whole thing - Don't put tables here — output them as markdown in your response text **Grid overflow:** `grid-template-columns: 1fr` has `min-width: auto` by default — children with large min-content push the column past the container. Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` to clamp. **Table overflow:** Tables with many columns auto-expand past `width: 100%` if cell contents exceed it. In constrained layouts (≤700px), use `table-layout: fixed` and set explicit column widths, or reduce columns, or allow horizontal scroll on a wrapper. ### Mockup presentation Contained mockups — mobile screens, chat threads, single cards, modals, small UI components — should sit on a background surface (`var(--surface-1)` container with `border-radius: 12px` and padding, or a device frame) so they don't float naked on the widget canvas. Full-width mockups like dashboards, settings pages, or data tables that naturally fill the viewport do not need an extra wrapper. ### 1. Interactive explainer — learn how something works *"Explain how compound interest works" / "Teach me about sorting algorithms"* Use HTML for the interactive controls — sliders, buttons, live state displays, charts. Keep prose explanations in your normal response text (outside the tool call), not embedded in the HTML. No card wrapper. Whitespace is the container. ```html <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <label style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">Years</label> <input type="range" min="1" max="40" value="20" id="years" style="flex: 1;" /> <span style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 500; min-width: 24px;" id="years-out">20</span> </div> <div style="display: flex; align-items: baseline; gap: 8px; margin: 0 0 1.5rem;"> <span style="font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-secondary);">£1,000 →</span> <span style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: 500;" id="result">£3,870</span> </div> <div style="margin: 2rem 0; position: relative; height: 240px;"> <canvas id="chart"></canvas> </div> ``` Use `sendPrompt()` to let users ask follow-ups: `sendPrompt('What if I increase the rate to 10%?')` ### 2. Compare options — decision making *"Compare pricing and features of these products" / "Help me choose between React and Vue"* Use HTML. Side-by-side card grid for options. Highlight differences with semantic colors. Interactive elements for filtering or weighting. - Each option in a card. Use badges for key differentiators. A leading Tabler icon (`<i class="ti ti-NAME">` at 20px, `aria-hidden`) anchors each option visually — pick the most apt name per option. - Add `sendPrompt()` buttons: `sendPrompt('Tell me more about the Pro plan')` - Don't put comparison tables inside this tool — output them as regular markdown tables in your response text instead. The tool is for the visual card grid only. - When one option is recommended or "most popular", accent its card with `border: 2px solid var(--border-accent)` only (2px is deliberate — the only exception to the 0.5px rule, used to accent featured items) — keep the same background and border as the other cards. Add a small badge (e.g. "Most popular") above or inside the card header using `background: var(--bg-accent); color: var(--text-accent); font-size: 12px; padding: 4px 12px; border-radius: var(--radius)`. ### 3. Data record — bounded UI object *"Show me a Salesforce contact card" / "Create a receipt for this order"* Use HTML. Wrap the entire thing in a single raised card. All content is sans-serif since it's pure UI. Use an avatar/initials circle for people (see example below). ```html <div style="background: var(--surface-2); border-radius: 12px; border: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding: 1rem 1.25rem;"> <div style="display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px;"> <div style="width: 44px; height: 44px; border-radius: 50%; background: var(--bg-accent); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-weight: 500; font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-accent);">MR</div> <div> <p style="font-weight: 500; font-size: 15px; margin: 0;">Maya Rodriguez</p> <p style="font-size: 13px; color: var(--text-secondary); margin: 0;">VP of Engineering</p> </div> </div> <div style="border-top: 0.5px solid var(--border); padding-top: 12px;"> <table style="width: 100%; font-size: 13px;"> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-mail" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Email</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0; color: var(--text-accent);">m.rodriguez@acme.com</td></tr> <tr><td style="color: var(--text-secondary); padding: 4px 0;"><i class="ti ti-phone" style="font-size:16px; vertical-align:-2px; margin-right:6px" aria-hidden="true"></i>Phone</td><td style="text-align: right; padding: 4px 0;">+1 (415) 555-0172</td></tr> </table> </div> </div> ``` ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. References below to `CdsRoot`, `Button`, or Tailwind utilities belong to the React build; in vanilla, read a utility like `bg-surface-1` as the underlying `var(--surface-1)`. ## Rules ### Token rule Reference purpose-layer tokens as CSS custom properties: ```css /* GOOD */ background: var(--surface-1); color: var(--text-secondary); border: 0.5px solid var(--border); /* BAD — raw hex, invisible in dark mode */ color: #3d3d3a; ``` | Property | Tokens | | ---------- | ------ | | Background | `--surface-{0..3,popover,panel}` · `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning,pro,neutral}` · `--fill-{role}` | | Text | `--text-{primary,secondary,muted,disabled}` · `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning,pro}` · `--on-{role}` | | Border | `--border` (default hairline) · `--border-{strong,stronger}` · `--border-{role}` | | Sizing | `--h-control` · `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}` · `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}` · `--radius` | | Typography | `--font-{sans,mono,voice}` · `--font-size-{caption,footnote,body,code,heading,title}` | | Shadow | `--shadow-{sm,md,lg,popover}` | | Motion | `--dur-{fast,snap,base,slow}` · `--ease-{out,snap,overshoot}` | ### Dark mode rule Dark mode is `[data-mode="dark"]` on `:root` (or `prefers-color-scheme: dark` with no explicit `data-mode`). All tokens flip automatically — never hardcode a dark-mode override. ### Muted text rule Secondary copy uses `color: var(--text-muted)`, **never** `opacity` — opacity multiplies against the background and drifts per-surface. ### Accent rule At most **one** accent-filled (`variant="primary"`) Button per view; siblings use `secondary` or `ghost`. The `brand` (clay) role is reserved for Claude-initiated actions — send, generate — never ordinary user CTAs. ### Restraint rule Default to the quieter, lighter option — "too cluttered" is the most common design note. - `secondary` is the default Button; `primary` / `brand` read as aggressive — don't reach for them in popovers, banners, or dense tool/canvas surfaces. - Avoid disabled buttons. Keep them enabled and respond on use (disabled controls are low-contrast and show no tooltip on touch); use `disabledReason` only when you genuinely must disable. - Dense lists: bordered rows, not rounded-rect cards. - Don't oversize padding, tooltips, or badges — trust the density scale. ### Elevation rule `surface-0` is the page canvas (via `--page-bg`); `1`/`2`/`3` step above it. At most **two** floating elevations (`panel` / `popover`) on screen at once. A third floating layer means `Dialog`, not popover-on-popover. Flat in-flow tiles (`rounded-card bg-surface-1 shadow-card-ring`) have no depth and don't count toward this limit. --- ## CDS principles How something feels like Claude — the philosophy behind the tokens. Tokens tell you _what_ you can use; the [Rules](../CLAUDE.md#rules) tell you _how_ to apply them. These principles tell you _why_. ## Claude-native cds is designed to be authored _by_ Claude as much as _for_ Claude's products. The `CLAUDE.md` you're reading is the system prompt; component docs are structured for retrieval; utilities are named so a model can guess them; the GenerateDemo page proves the loop works. A design system an LLM can use fluently is one humans can use fluently too. ## Clay is Claude's color `brand` (clay) is reserved for what Claude does — send, generate, the spark mark. User-driven primary actions take the neutral `accent` blue; everything else stays gray. Holding clay back to a single role is what lets it carry meaning instead of becoming wallpaper. ## Serif is Claude's voice Claude's responses render in serif; the surrounding chrome stays sans. Typography signals who's speaking before a word is read. cds ships `--font-voice` (the `font-voice` utility) for response surfaces. ## Density adapts to the surface Console, claude.ai and antfarm share the same components — `compact` for dev tools and power users, `comfortable` for consumer apps. Density is one switch on `CdsRoot`, not a per-component prop, so a product can change its feel without forking a single component. ## Built to be extended Every component takes `className`, every token is a public CSS var, and compound parts (`.Root`, `.Item`, `.Trigger`) sit under the porcelain helpers. The system expects you to compose past it — wrap, restyle, slot arbitrary children — not fork it. ## Restraint over options One accent per view, one elevation step, t-shirt sizes instead of 0–12 scales. Fewer decisions at the call site means fewer ways for two screens to drift apart — consistency comes from removing knobs, not policing them. ## CDS tokens Every visual decision in `@ant/cds` resolves to a `--*` CSS custom property. The TypeScript source of truth lives under `packages/cds/tokens/`; `yarn gen:tokens` emits the shipped CSS at [`src/generated/tokens.css`](../src/generated/tokens.css). Tokens are layered so that a single edit at the bottom (a hex value) propagates through ramps, roles, and purposes without touching component code. ## The layer model ``` 1. Base palette --{hue}-{stop} literal hex, mode-stable (gray, red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, violet, magenta) 2. Theme ramps --neutral-N gray-N in light, gray-(900-N) in dark --alpha-N neutral-900 @ fixed opacity (so it flips too) 3. Elevation --surface-{0..3} 0 = darkest, 3 = lightest, in BOTH modes 4. Purpose --surface-{popover, what components actually consume; includes the panel}, --text-*, role mappings ({fill|bg|border|text}-{role}) --fill-*, --on-* — page-bg --page-bg hook the host app sets to its canvas color 5. Density --h-control*, px values; remapped by [data-density] --pad-*, --gap-*, --radius, --font-size-*, --leading-* 6. Motion --dur-*, durations + easing curves (mode/density-invariant) --ease-* ``` **Components only read layer 4 (and 5 for sizing).** Layers 1–3 are wiring. --- ## 1. Base palette Literal hex values, mode-stable — `gray-500` is the same pixel in light and dark. Nine hues share one 36-stop grid (0, 10–100 by 10, 150–800 by 50, 810–900 by 10); every hue anchors 0 = `#ffffff` and 900 = `#0b0b0b`. Rarely referenced directly — reach for layers 2–4 and let them resolve here. --- ## 2. Theme ramps `--neutral-N` is `gray-N` in light and `gray-(900-N)` in dark, so `neutral-0` is always the near-background end and `neutral-900` the near-foreground end. Use it for "contrast against the page" (text, borders, fills); use `gray-*` when you mean a specific pixel value regardless of mode. `--alpha-N` is `neutral-900` at fixed opacity — a black wash in light, a white wash in dark, without per-mode overrides. --- ## 3. Elevation | Token | Light | Dark | Use case | | ----------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------ | | `--surface-0` | `gray-20` | `gray-890` | Page | | `--surface-1` | `gray-10` | `gray-830` | In-flow card | | `--surface-2` | `gray-0` | `gray-750` | Panel | | `--surface-3` | `gray-0` | `gray-700` | Popover | The ordinal is absolute lightness in both modes: 0 is the darkest, 3 the lightest. `--surface-panel` and `--surface-popover` alias levels 2 and 3. Purpose **This is the layer components consume.** ### Roles Each role maps a semantic meaning to a hue. Brand uses named `clay-emphasized` / hover `clay` (not hue stops). | Role | Hue | Tokens | | --------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `accent` | blue | `--fill-accent{,-hover}`, `--bg-accent`, `--border-accent`, `--text-accent` | | `brand` | clay | `--fill-brand{,-hover}`, `--on-brand` (fill-only — no text/bg/border) | | `danger` | red | `--fill-danger{,-hover}`, `--bg-danger`, `--border-danger`, `--text-danger` | | `success` | green | `--fill-success{,-hover}`, `--bg-success`, `--border-success`, `--text-success` | | `warning` | yellow | `--fill-warning{,-hover}`, `--bg-warning`, `--border-warning`, `--text-warning` | | `pro` | purple | `--fill-pro{,-hover}`, `--bg-pro`, `--border-pro`, `--text-pro` | #### `git-*` roles Diff and PR/CR-state colors — `added`, `removed`, `modified`, `conflicting`, `merged`, `closed`, `draft`, plus `opened`/`queued` as aliases of `added`/`modified`. Each carries the full `text` / `fill{,-hover}` / `bg` / `border` / `on` suite. Light enough that `text-{role}` (hue-600) reads against it: a danger banner is `bg-danger` + `text-danger`. `fill-{role}` is the saturated solid (hue-450) for interactive controls — button, checkbox, toggle. Too dark for `text-{role}`, so it pairs with `on-{role}` (gray-0 / gray-900) instead; the 450 stop is chosen for WCAG contrast against `on-*`. | | Background | Foreground | Example | | ----- | ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | | Tint | `bg-{role}` | `text-{role}` | Banner, Badge | | Solid | `fill-{role}` | `on-{role}` | Button | The token name encodes the pairing: use `bg-*` when the hue is ambient context behind body text; `fill-*` when the hue _is_ the control surface. ### Purpose tokens | Token | Value (light) | Use case | | ---------------------------- | `alpha-3` | Emphasized divider | | `--border-stronger` | `neutral-900 / 40%` | Heavy divider | | `--fill-primary` | `neutral-900` | Primary button bg | | `--fill-primary-hover` | `neutral-750` | | | `--fill-secondary` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.1)` | Secondary button bg | | `--fill-secondary-hover` | `alpha-1` | | | `--fill-secondary-ring` | `border` (light) / transparent (dark) | Secondary button ring | | `--fill-field` | `hsl(0 0% 100% / 0.5)` (light) / `fill-secondary` (dark) | Field control bg (TextInput, TextArea, Combobox) | | `--fill-ghost-hover` | `alpha-1` | Ghost button hover bg | | `--fill-control` | `alpha-2` | Avatar fallback bg | | `--fill-control-hover` | `alpha-3` | | | `--fill-disabled` | `alpha-1` | Disabled control bg | | `--on-primary` | `neutral-0` | Text on `fill-primary` | | `--on-accent` | `gray-0` | Text on `accent` | | `--on-brand` | `gray-0` | Text on `brand` | | `--on-danger` | `gray-0` | Text on `danger` | | `--on-success` | `gray-900` | Text on `success` | | `--on-warning` | `gray-900` | Text on `warning` | | `--on-pro` | `gray-0` | Text on `pro` | | `--focus-shadow` | `0 0 0 1px accent, 0 0 6px 1px bg-accent` | `focus-visible` ring | | `--shadow-sm` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Low elevation | | `--shadow-md` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Card / panel | | `--shadow-lg` | two-layer via `--shadow-color` | Dialog / sheet | | `--shadow-popover` | `0 8px 24px /12%, 0 2px 6px /8%` | Menu, dropdown popups | | `--surface-popover` | `surface-3` | Named alias | | `--surface-panel` | `surface-2` | Named alias | `--shadow-sm/md/lg` are two-layer composites (contact + diffused drop) driven by `--shadow-color`, which deepens to `black/24%` in dark mode (epitaxy parity). `--shadow-popover` is a fixed two-layer literal tuned for floating menus. --- ## CDS content How to write the words that go inside cds components. Tokens decide how the UI _looks_; this decides how it _sounds_. The voice is **intelligent, warm, unvarnished, and collaborative** — your smartest friend explaining something in plain terms. Friendly lives in the copy, not in extra chrome. ## Mechanics - **Sentence case everywhere.** Buttons, headings, tabs, labels, menu items. "Save changes", not "Save Changes". Title Case is for proper nouns only (Claude, Opus, Anthropic Console). - **No terminal punctuation on labels and headings.** Helper text, descriptions, and empty-state body copy _do_ end with a period. - **Use contractions.** "Can't", "you'll", "it's". Conversational, not stiff. - **Active voice, verb first.** "Delete project", not "Project deletion". - **Ellipsis = in progress only.** "Claude is thinking…". Not for trailing off, not for menu suffixes. - **No ampersands.** Spell out "and". - **Serial comma.** "Chats, projects, and artifacts." ## Pronouns UI speaks as the product, not as Claude and not as the user. | Context | Use | Example | | ---------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | User's things | **your** | "Your projects" — never "My projects" | | Confirmations | none / past tense | "Saved", "Got it" — never "I saved it" | | Errors | **you / your** | "Your session expired" — never "I couldn't…" | | Claude (in chat) | **I** | Reserved for the chat surface; system UI never says "I" | ## Words to avoid | Skip | Why | Instead | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------- | | "successfully" | The success toast _is_ the success | "File uploaded" | | "please" | UI isn't asking a favor | "Enter a name" | | "Click here" / "Tap to…" | Link text should name the destination | "Read the docs" | | "!" on system copy | Reads as shouty | "Settings saved" | | "leverage", "seamless", "unlock", "empower" | Corporate filler | Say what it does | | "simply", "just", "easy" | Presumes — and condescends | Cut it | ## Patterns **Buttons / CTAs** — verb first, 1–3 words, sentence case, no punctuation. "Create project", "Upgrade to Pro". Not "OK", "Submit", or "Click to continue". **Errors** — say what happened, then what to do. One sentence, no "Error:" prefix, no first person. "That name's already taken. Try another." Never surface raw exception strings. **Empty states** — an invitation, not an apology. Headline names the space ("Start your first project"), one-line body explains it, CTA is a verb ("Create project"). Skip "Nothing here yet." **Placeholders** — a real example of valid input ("name@company.com", "Summarize this document"). No "e.g." prefix, don't repeat the field label. **Links** — describe where they go ("Learn more", "View pricing"). Keep them at the end of the sentence; punctuation sits outside the link. ## Do / Don't | Do | Don't | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | "File uploaded" | "Your file was uploaded successfully!" | | "Enter a workspace name" | "Please enter a workspace name." | | "Couldn't connect to Slack. Retry" | "Error: I was unable to connect." | | "Your projects" | "My projects" | | "Create project" | "Click Here To Get Started" | | "Connect Slack" | "Add the Slack Connector" |

content.text:
That mockup above is the **same data your app already has** — just restyled. Nothing was changed or deployed; it's purely a "what it could look like" preview.

## The key point
Notice this is still exactly your stack — dark theme, orange accent, the same dashboard content. What makes it feel current vs. dated is **only CSS**: softer rounded cards, hairline borders instead of heavy ones, more breathing room, a cleaner type hierarchy (big quiet numbers, muted labels), subtle status pills, and a slim icon rail. **None of that requires leaving Astro** — it's a stylesheet-level change.

So the honest recommendation stands: a **design refresh**, not a framework migration. The refresh gets you the modern look in a fraction of the time and with zero risk to the backend/financial logic. A framework swap would be weeks of work that, by itself, wouldn't change the look at all.

## If/when you want to actually do it (no rush)
Because your app already reads from a central set of CSS variables, a lot of this can be rolled out globally by updating those tokens (palette, radius, shadows, spacing, fonts) — lifting every page at once — then polishing the shared components (cards, tables, buttons, nav).

For now I've changed nothing. Whenever you're ready, tell me and I can:
- Restyle **one real page** in the actual app so you can compare side-by-side before committing, or
- Do a **global token refresh** that modernizes everything in one pass, or
- Iterate on this mockup first (different accent, spacing, layout) until the direction feels right.

Want me to tweak anything about this preview — accent color, density, layout — so it matches the vibe you're after?

content.text:
This is the right move — and I found the critical gap: **`/opt/soulpilates` isn't even a Git repo.** Every change this session (and presumably before) has been unversioned edits made directly on the live server. So step zero is version control; everything else builds on it.

Here's a practical plan tailored to your actual setup (single VPS, Docker Compose, and you already have the **Studio Nexis fork as a proven "parallel stack on the same VPS" template**).

## The target workflow
```
work locally / on a branch  →  deploy to STAGING (own DB, test keys)  →  test
        →  push to GitHub  →  merge to main  →  deploy to PRODUCTION (live)
```

## Step 1 — Put the code under version control (do this first)
1. `git init` in `/opt/soulpilates`, add a `.gitignore` (exclude `prod.env`, secrets, `*.bak`, build artifacts, `MuscleMapJS` if vendored, etc.).
2. Commit the current state, create a **private GitHub repo**, push it.
3. Branch model: **`main` = production**, and you do work on **feature branches** (or a `develop` branch) that get merged into `main` only after passing on staging.
> Secrets never go in Git — `prod.env`/`staging.env` stay on the server (or in GitHub Actions secrets).

## Step 2 — Stand up a staging stack (parallel, same VPS)
Mirror how Studio Nexis is isolated — a second Docker Compose stack that shares nothing with prod:
- **Own containers** (`soulpilates-staging-*`), **own ports** (e.g. backend `8491`, frontend `3819`, mongo `27217`), **own images** (`soulpilates/backend:staging`).
- **Own subdomain** → `staging.soulpilates.com.vn` (add an nginx server block + cert), ideally behind HTTP basic-auth so it's not public.
- **Own `staging.env`** with its **own DB name**, **Stripe TEST keys**, and email **TEST mode / redirect inbox** — so testing can never email real customers or charge real cards (that redirect mechanism already exists in `EmailService`).
- Cost: ~free (same box). Tradeoff: shares CPU/RAM with prod. If you'd rather fully isolate, a small separate $10–20/mo VPS for staging is cleaner — but same-VPS is fine to start.

## Step 3 — Sync the database into staging (not shared!)
Staging gets its **own copy** of the data, refreshed on demand — it must never write to the live DB.
- A small `sync-staging-db.sh`: `mongodump` from the prod mongo → `mongorestore --drop` into the staging mongo.
- Run it **manually before a test session** or on a nightly cron.
- Strongly recommended: an **anonymization pass** after restore (scramble customer emails/phones/names) so real PII isn't sitting in the less-locked staging env and test emails can't reach real people.

## Step 4 — Publishing (deploy automation)
Two levels, start simple:
- **Now (scripts on the VPS):** `deploy-staging.sh` (`git checkout <branch>` → build `:staging` images → `docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml up -d`) and `deploy-prod.sh` (`git checkout main && git pull` → build `:latest` → prod compose up). This replaces the ad-hoc manual rebuilds.
- **Later (GitHub Actions):** push to a branch → CI SSHes into the VPS and runs the staging deploy; merging to `main` → CI runs the prod deploy. Fully "push to GitHub → auto-publish."

## Two things to flag
- Your `SoulPilates.Tests` project was noted as non-compiling — worth reviving so CI can actually run tests before deploy. Otherwise "testing" is only manual on staging.
- Keep the **`--build-arg PUBLIC_API_URL`** distinct per environment (`https://staging.soulpilates.com.vn` vs prod) — same gotcha as prod.

## Want me to bootstrap it?
I can do the mechanical parts right now, safely (they don't touch running prod):
1. **Initialize Git** — add a proper `.gitignore`, make the first commit of the current codebase (so you finally have a baseline + history of this session's changes).
2. **Write the staging Compose file** (`docker-compose.staging.yml`) + a `staging.env` template with its own ports/DB and test-mode integrations.
3. **Write `sync-staging-db.sh`** (dump→restore, with an optional anonymize step) and `deploy-staging.sh` / `deploy-prod.sh`.

You'd still need to do the account-level bits yourself (create the GitHub repo + push, point the `staging.` DNS/subdomain, add Stripe test keys). Want me to start with **Step 1 (Git init + first commit)** so your work is finally versioned, and then scaffold the staging stack?

content.content:
branch: main
=== prod compose (full, to mirror) ===
# Soul Pilates — PRODUCTION Stack
#
#  Assumes you've copied soulpilates-backend-latest.tar.gz and
#  soulpilates-frontend-latest.tar.gz onto the host and loaded them with:
#    docker load < soulpilates-backend-latest.tar.gz
#    docker load < soulpilates-frontend-latest.tar.gz
#
#  Then:
#    cp prod.env.sample prod.env  # edit secrets
#    docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
#
#  External access (mongosh / redis-cli from your dev machine):
#    MongoDB → host:${MONGO_PUBLIC_PORT}   (default 27117)
#    Redis   → host:${REDIS_PUBLIC_PORT}   (default 6479)
#    Both are auth-protected. Restrict access at the firewall to trusted IPs:
#      ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 27117
#      ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 6479
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

services:

  mongo:
    image: mongo:8
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-mongo
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Exposed on a non-default host port so the operator can run mongosh
      # from a dev machine. Auth is mandatory (MONGO_USER / MONGO_PASSWORD).
      # Restrict via firewall: ufw allow from <trusted-ip> to any port ${MONGO_PUBLIC_PORT}
      - "127.0.0.1:${MONGO_PUBLIC_PORT:-27117}:27017"
    environment:
      MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME: ${MONGO_USER}
      MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MONGO_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ./data/mongo:/data/db
    command: ["mongod", "--bind_ip_all"]
    networks: [internal]

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-redis
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Exposed on a non-default host port for direct redis-cli access.
      # Protected by REDIS_PASSWORD via --requirepass.
      # Restrict via firewall: ufw allow from <trusted-ip> to any port ${REDIS_PUBLIC_PORT}
      - "127.0.0.1:${REDIS_PUBLIC_PORT:-6479}:6379"
    volumes:
      - ./data/redis:/data
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--requirepass", "${REDIS_PASSWORD}"]
    networks: [internal]

  rustfs-volume-init:
    image: alpine:3.20
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-rustfs-init
    volumes:
      - ./data/rustfs:/data
    command: sh -c "chown -R 10001:10001 /data"
    restart: "no"

  rustfs:
    image: rustfs/rustfs:latest
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-rustfs
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6324:9000"      # S3 API — exposed so the public can fetch images
      - "127.0.0.1:6325:9001"
    environment:
      RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY: ${RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY}
      RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY: ${RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY}
      RUSTFS_CONSOLE_ENABLE: "true"
    volumes:
      - ./data/rustfs:/data
    depends_on:
      rustfs-volume-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    networks: [internal, public]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "--quiet", "--tries=1", "--spider", "http://localhost:9000/health"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 10s

  # One-shot that creates the soulpilates-public bucket (idempotent).
  # Runs after rustfs is healthy so it never races the S3 API startup.
  # Sets anonymous download policy so the frontend can fetch images directly.
  rustfs-bucket-init:
    image: minio/mc:latest
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-rustfs-bucket-init
    restart: "no"
    environment:
      RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY: ${RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY}
      RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY: ${RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY}
    entrypoint: >
      /bin/sh -c "
        mc alias set rustfs http://rustfs:9000 $$RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY $$RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY &&
        mc mb --ignore-existing rustfs/soulpilates-public &&
        mc anonymous set download rustfs/soulpilates-public &&
        echo 'Bucket soulpilates-public ready.'
      "
    depends_on:
      rustfs:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks: [internal]

  backend:
    image: soulpilates/backend:latest
    container_name: soulpilates-prod-backend
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8391:8080"
    environment:
      ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT: Production
      ASPNETCORE_URLS: http://+:8080
      MongoDbSettings__ConnectionString: "mongodb://${MONGO_USER}:${MONGO_PASSWORD}@mongo:27017/?authSource=admin"
      MongoDbSettings__DatabaseName: soulpilates
      JwtSettings__Secret: ${JWT_SECRET}
      # P4-S12 — optional previous-key slot for the rotation grace window.
      # Empty string is interpreted by Program.cs as "no previous key" (single-key mode).
      JwtSettings__PreviousSecret: ${JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET:-}
      StorageSettings__Endpoint: "http://rustfs:9000"
      StorageSettings__AccessKey: ${RUSTFS_ACCESS_KEY}
      StorageSettings__SecretKey: ${RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY}
      StorageSettings__PublicBucket: soulpilates-public
      StorageSettings__PublicUrlBase: ${PUBLIC_MEDIA_URL_BASE}
      StorageSettings__ForcePathStyle: "true"
      StripeSettings__SecretKey: ${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY}
      StripeSettings__PublishableKey: ${STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY}
      StripeSettings__WebhookSecret: ${STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET}
      StripeSettings__Enabled: ${STRIPE_ENABLED}
      # ───── SMTP / Email ─────
      SmtpSettings__Host: ${SMTP_HOST}
      SmtpSettings__Port: ${SMTP_PORT:-587}
      SmtpSettings__Username: ${SMTP_USERNAME}
      SmtpSettings__Password: ${SMTP_PASSWORD}
      SmtpSettings__FromEmail: ${SMTP_FROM_EMAIL}
      SmtpSettings__FromName: ${SMTP_FROM_NAME:-Soul Pilates Da Nang}
      SmtpSettings__Enabled: ${SMTP_ENABLED:-true}
      SmtpSettings__EmailRegisterVerificationEnabled: ${SMTP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION_ENABLED:-true}
      # Email test-mode safety net: when TestMode=true, real customers never get
      # mail — everything is redirected to TestRedirectTo (or dropped), except
      # addresses in TestAllowlist which still receive the real email.
      SmtpSettings__TestMode: ${SMTP_TEST_MODE:-false}
      SmtpSettings__TestRedirectTo: ${SMTP_TEST_REDIRECT_TO:-}
      SmtpSettings__TestAllowlist: ${SMTP_TEST_ALLOWLIST:-}
      # ───── Meta (Facebook/Instagram) Pixel + Conversions API ─────
      MetaTracking__PixelId: ${META_PIXEL_ID:-}
      MetaTracking__AccessToken: ${META_CAPI_TOKEN:-}
      MetaTracking__TestEventCode: ${META_CAPI_TEST_CODE:-}
      MetaTracking__Enabled: ${META_TRACKING_ENABLED:-true}
      # ───── TikTok Pixel + Events API ─────
      TiktokTracking__PixelCode: ${TIKTOK_PIXEL_CODE:-}
      TiktokTracking__AccessToken: ${TIKTOK_EVENTS_TOKEN:-}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Copy the PRODUCTION database into the STAGING database.
#   • Read-only on production (mongodump only).
#   • Restores with --drop into the staging mongo (own instance).
#   • Anonymizes PII by default so real customer emails/phones never live in
#     staging and test emails can't reach real people. Also blanks Stripe keys.
#
# Usage:   scripts/sync-staging-db.sh            # sync + anonymize (default)
#          ANONYMIZE=0 scripts/sync-staging-db.sh # exact copy, no scrubbing
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
set -euo pipefail

PROD_ENV="${PROD_ENV:-/opt/soulpilates/prod.env}"
STG_ENV="${STG_ENV:-/opt/soulpilates-staging/staging.env}"
PROD_MONGO="${PROD_MONGO:-soulpilates-prod-mongo}"
STG_MONGO="${STG_MONGO:-soulpilates-staging-mongo}"
ANONYMIZE="${ANONYMIZE:-1}"
DB="soulpilates"

get() { grep -oP "(?<=^$1=).*" "$2"; }
PMU=$(get MONGO_USER "$PROD_ENV"); PMP=$(get MONGO_PASSWORD "$PROD_ENV")
SMU=$(get MONGO_USER "$STG_ENV");  SMP=$(get MONGO_PASSWORD "$STG_ENV")

tmp=$(mktemp /tmp/sp-sync.XXXX.gz)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT

echo "→ dumping production DB (read-only)…"
docker exec -e U="$PMU" -e P="$PMP" "$PROD_MONGO" sh -c \
  'mongodump -u "$U" -p "$P" --authenticationDatabase admin --db '"$DB"' --archive --gzip' > "$tmp"
echo "   dump size: $(du -h "$tmp" | cut -f1)"

echo "→ restoring into staging DB (--drop)…"
docker exec -i -e U="$SMU" -e P="$SMP" "$STG_MONGO" sh -c \
  'mongorestore -u "$U" -p "$P" --authenticationDatabase admin --archive --gzip --drop' < "$tmp"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Copy the PRODUCTION database into the STAGING database.
#   • Read-only on production (mongodump only).
#   • Restores with --drop into the staging mongo (own instance).
#   • Anonymizes PII by default so real customer emails/phones never live in
#     staging and test emails can't reach real people. Also blanks Stripe keys.
#
# Usage:   scripts/sync-staging-db.sh            # sync + anonymize (default)
#          ANONYMIZE=0 scripts/sync-staging-db.sh # exact copy, no scrubbing
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
set -euo pipefail

PROD_ENV="${PROD_ENV:-/opt/soulpilates/prod.env}"
STG_ENV="${STG_ENV:-/opt/soulpilates-staging/staging.env}"
PROD_MONGO="${PROD_MONGO:-soulpilates-prod-mongo}"
STG_MONGO="${STG_MONGO:-soulpilates-staging-mongo}"
ANONYMIZE="${ANONYMIZE:-1}"
DB="soulpilates"

get() { grep -oP "(?<=^$1=).*" "$2"; }
PMU=$(get MONGO_USER "$PROD_ENV"); PMP=$(get MONGO_PASSWORD "$PROD_ENV")
SMU=$(get MONGO_USER "$STG_ENV");  SMP=$(get MONGO_PASSWORD "$STG_ENV")

tmp=$(mktemp /tmp/sp-sync.XXXX.gz)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT

echo "→ dumping production DB (read-only)…"
docker exec -e U="$PMU" -e P="$PMP" "$PROD_MONGO" sh -c \
  'mongodump -u "$U" -p "$P" --authenticationDatabase admin --db '"$DB"' --archive --gzip' > "$tmp"
echo "   dump size: $(du -h "$tmp" | cut -f1)"

docker exec -i -e U="$SMU" -e P="$SMP" "$STG_MONGO" sh -c \
  'mongorestore -u "$U" -p "$P" --authenticationDatabase admin --archive --gzip --drop' < "$tmp"

if [ "$ANONYMIZE" = "1" ]; then
  echo "→ scrubbing PII + secrets in staging…"
  docker exec -e U="$SMU" -e P="$SMP" "$STG_MONGO" mongosh --quiet -u "$SMU" -p "$SMP" --authenticationDatabase admin --eval '
    var db = db.getSiblingDB("soulpilates");

    i = 0; db.CustomerAccounts.find({}).forEach(function(c){ i++; db.CustomerAccounts.updateOne({_id:c._id},{$set:{Email:"cust"+i+"@staging.local"}}); });
    db.Attendances.updateMany({}, {$set:{ClientEmail:"attendee@staging.local", ClientPhone:"0900000000"}});
    db.EmailLogs.deleteMany({});
    db.Settings.updateMany({}, {$set:{StripeEnabled:false, StripeSecretKeyEncrypted:"", StripePublishableKeyEncrypted:"", StripeWebhookSecretEncrypted:""}});
    print("   scrubbed clients/customers/attendees emails+phones, cleared email log + stripe keys");

# Staging & release workflow — setup guide

This repo now supports a proper **staging → GitHub → production** flow so you
never develop directly on the live system again.

```
edit on a branch (staging dir)  →  deploy-staging + test
   →  push to GitHub  →  merge to main  →  deploy-prod
```

## What's already been set up
- **Full backup** taken before any changes → `/opt/backups/soulpilates-<timestamp>/`
  (`db-mongodump.archive.gz` + `full-soulpilates.tar.gz`, verified).
- **Git repo** initialized at `/opt/soulpilates` with a baseline commit; branches
  `main` (production) and `develop` (work). Secrets/data are gitignored.
- **Staging stack files**: `docker-compose.staging.yml`, `staging.env.sample`.
- **Scripts**: `scripts/deploy-staging.sh`, `scripts/deploy-prod.sh`,
  `scripts/sync-staging-db.sh`.

## One-time setup you need to do (needs your accounts / DNS)

### 1. Push the repo to GitHub
```bash
cd /opt/soulpilates
# create a PRIVATE repo on github.com first, then:
git remote add origin git@github.com:<you>/soulpilates-crm.git
git push -u origin main
git push origin develop
```

### 2. Create the staging working directory (separate from live)
Staging is a **second checkout** so editing/testing never touches the live source:
```bash
git clone /opt/soulpilates /opt/soulpilates-staging      # or clone from GitHub
cd /opt/soulpilates-staging
git checkout develop
cp staging.env.sample staging.env       # then fill in — see step 3
```

### 3. Fill in `staging.env` (own secrets, NOT prod's)
Generate fresh values so staging is fully isolated:
```bash
# JWT + passwords
openssl rand -hex 32          # → JWT_SECRET
openssl rand -hex 16          # → MONGO_PASSWORD / REDIS_PASSWORD / RUSTFS_SECRET_KEY
# VAPID keypair for web push (or reuse a throwaway pair)
```
Set `SMTP_TEST_REDIRECT_TO=` to your own inbox (test emails go there, never to
customers). Keep `STRIPE_ENABLED=false` unless testing payments with `sk_test_…`.

### 4. Point a staging subdomain at it (nginx + cert)
Add DNS `staging.soulpilates.com.vn` → this server, then an nginx server block
(mirror the prod one) with a TLS cert, proxying:
- `/api` and `/soulpilates-public` → the backend/rustfs (`127.0.0.1:8491`, `:6424`)
- everything else → the frontend (`127.0.0.1:3819`)

Recommended: protect the whole staging host with HTTP basic-auth so it isn't public.

### 5. Bring staging up + load data
```bash
cd /opt/soulpilates-staging
scripts/deploy-staging.sh develop     # builds :staging images, starts the stack
/opt/soulpilates/scripts/sync-staging-db.sh   # copies prod data in (PII scrubbed)
```

## Day-to-day workflow
1. In `/opt/soulpilates-staging`, branch off develop: `git checkout -b feature/x`.
2. Make changes there and `scripts/deploy-staging.sh feature/x` to test.
3. Commit + push: `git push origin feature/x`; open a PR into `main` on GitHub.
4. After review/merge, publish live: on **`/opt/soulpilates`** run
   `scripts/deploy-prod.sh` (pulls `main`, rebuilds, recreates the app containers).

> The live production dir (`/opt/soulpilates`) should only ever be updated via
> `deploy-prod.sh` (i.e. from merged `main`), not hand-edited.

## Restore from backup (if ever needed)
```bash
BK=/opt/backups/soulpilates-<timestamp>
# DB only:
docker exec -i soulpilates-prod-mongo sh -c 'mongorestore -u USER -p PASS \
  --authenticationDatabase admin --archive --gzip --drop' < "$BK/db-mongodump.archive.gz"
# Everything (code + configs + data): extract the full archive
tar xzf "$BK/full-soulpilates.tar.gz" -C /some/restore/path
```

message.content: so everything that happens in the live system db like new clients, bookings etc. will be synced in the staging system however it wont write anything to the live system db, correct?

content.text:
Half right — let me correct the important part so you don't get caught out.

## ✅ Correct: staging never writes to the live DB
Staging has its **own separate MongoDB** (its own container, its own `data-staging/` volume). The sync is strictly **one-way and read-only on production** (`mongodump` only reads prod; the restore only writes into the *staging* DB). Nothing staging does — test bookings, edits, deletes — can ever touch the live database. That part is exactly as you said.

## ⚠️ Not automatic — the sync is a manual snapshot, not live replication
This is the misconception: it is **not** a continuous, live sync. New live clients/bookings do **not** automatically appear in staging. Staging only gets fresh data **when you run the sync script** (`scripts/sync-staging-db.sh`). Between runs, staging is frozen at the last snapshot.

Two things that follow from that:
- **Re-syncing overwrites staging.** The script does a `mongorestore --drop` — it wipes the staging DB and replaces it with a fresh copy of prod. So any test data you created in staging gets discarded on the next sync. That's intentional (gives you a clean, realistic dataset to test against) — just know it's destructive to staging.
- **Staging data is anonymized.** The sync scrubs customer emails/phones and clears Stripe keys, so staging isn't holding real PII. The numbers/structure are real; the contact details are fake.

So the accurate mental model:
```
LIVE DB  ──(you run sync, read-only)──►  STAGING DB   (overwrites staging)
LIVE DB  ◄─── never ───  STAGING DB      (staging can't write back)
```

## If you want it closer to "always fresh"
I can set up a **nightly cron** that auto-runs the sync (e.g., 3 AM) so staging is never more than a day stale — without you remembering to run it. That's the usual sweet spot for a test environment.

(True live-continuous replication is also technically possible via MongoDB change streams, but it's overkill for staging, adds moving parts, and would fight the "clean snapshot" model — I'd not recommend it here.)

Want me to add the nightly auto-sync cron? And should I still add the basic-auth lock on the staging URL I mentioned?

message.content: is it possible to send all fresh data to realtime to staging db?

content.text:
Yes, it's technically possible — but there's a fundamental catch you should understand before we go down that road, because "real-time sync" and "a testing environment you can write to" are actually in tension.

## The core tension
A staging environment is useful because **you can make changes in it** — create test bookings, try edits, break things safely. But real-time replication continuously pushes production's state into staging. Those two goals fight each other:

- **If staging live-mirrors prod**, it's effectively **read-only** — every test change you make gets overwritten (or conflicts) the moment prod changes. You'd lose the ability to actually *test*.
- **If staging is writable** (what you want for testing), then streaming prod data in on top of your test changes creates conflicts and clobbers your work.

So real-time is only the right tool if you want a **read-only live mirror** (e.g. to *view* current data), not a place to develop and test.

## The technical options (and their costs)
1. **MongoDB Change Streams** — a small service tails prod's changes and applies them to staging continuously. **Requires converting your production Mongo to a replica set** (it's currently standalone) — that's a config change + restart on the **live** database, which I'd be cautious about.
2. **Replica-set secondary / `mongosync`** — the "proper" continuous replication. Also requires prod to be a replica set, and a secondary is strictly **read-only** (can't test writes on it).
3. **Frequent scheduled snapshots** (cron every N minutes/hours) — "near-real-time" without touching prod's config or losing writability. This is the pragmatic middle ground.

## My honest recommendation
For a **testing** environment, you don't actually want real-time — you want *recent, stable, writable* data. The right tool is a **scheduled snapshot** (nightly, or as often as hourly). You get up-to-date data to test against, but a stable dataset that doesn't shift under you mid-test, and **zero changes to production**.

Real-time replication would mean touching your live DB's configuration and giving up the ability to test writes — a lot of downside for a testing box.

So — what's the actual goal? It changes the answer:

content.text:
That goal actually changes my recommendation — and in a good way, because **most of what you want, you already have without real-time replication.** Let me break it down honestly.

## For *seeing and diagnosing* live bugs — you don't need staging at all
When a client/booking bug happens in production, the fastest way to investigate is to look **directly at the live data and logs** — read-only, completely safe. That's exactly what I've done all session: queried the live DB to find the booking-counter drift, the KPI reset, the reimbursement issue, and pulled backend logs for errors. I can do that for any bug on demand, right now, without any new infrastructure. So "see the bug and fetch logs" = already fully available.

## For *reproducing and testing a fix* — an on-demand snapshot beats real-time
When you want to actually work on a fix, you want staging to hold **the current live state at that moment** — which is precisely what running the sync gives you (it's seconds). Then you have a **stable** copy to reproduce against and test the fix on, without production shifting under you mid-test. Continuous real-time would actually *hurt* here: it'd keep overwriting your test changes.

## True real-time *is* possible, but the cost is real and the fit is poor
To get continuous replication you'd have to:
1. **Convert your production MongoDB from standalone to a replica set** — that's a config change + restart of the **live** database (brief downtime, best in a maintenance window). It's a common, fairly low-risk operation, but it *is* touching prod.
2. Run a continuous sync (mongosync / change-streams applier).
3. And then staging becomes effectively **read-only** — writing a test fix there conflicts with the incoming live stream, so you'd have to pause replication to test anyway.

So you'd take on a production DB change and lose easy writability… to get something the on-demand snapshot already gives you for debugging. It's the wrong tool for this job.

## What I recommend (and can set up now)
The practical setup for "debug live issues with Claude":
1. **On-demand sync** — one command (`scripts/sync-staging-db.sh`) whenever a bug is reported → staging instantly mirrors current prod, ready to reproduce + fix.
2. **Hourly scheduled sync** (cron) — so staging is usually already fresh without you thinking about it.
3. **Direct prod diagnosis** — I read the live DB + logs directly for any incident (no waiting on a sync).

This gives you the whole workflow — see the bug live, reproduce it on current data, fix it in staging, then promote through GitHub → prod — with **zero production DB changes** and staging staying writable.

Want me to set up the **hourly auto-sync cron** (plus keep on-demand), and add the **basic-auth lock** on the staging URL? If after all this you still specifically want true real-time, I'll lay out the exact replica-set conversion steps and the risks so you can decide with eyes open — but I don't think you'll need it.

content.text:
Yes — **that's the entire point of staging.** Both visual changes (the modern dark redesign we mocked up, CSS, layouts, Astro pages) and logical changes (C# services, controllers, business logic) get made and tested there first, safely, against a real copy of your data — then promoted to live only once you're happy.

## How it works now (and how I'll work with you going forward)
There are **two independent pipelines**, flowing opposite directions:

```
DATA:   live DB  ──(sync, read-only)──►  staging DB
CODE:   staging  ──(GitHub main)──►  live      ← your changes flow THIS way
```

So staging gets **prod's data** to test against, and your **code changes** flow the other way (staging → reviewed → live). They never cross.

## The concrete flow for a change
1. I make the edits in **`/opt/soulpilates-staging`** (the staging working dir, on a `develop`/feature branch) — **not** in the live `/opt/soulpilates`.
2. I rebuild the `:staging` images and restart the staging containers → the change is live at **`https://staging.soulpilates.com.vn`** in a minute or two.
3. **You review it there** on the real staging site with real data.
4. Once you approve, we commit + push → merge to `main` on GitHub → I run `deploy-prod.sh` on the live box to publish it.
5. If you don't like it, we just iterate on staging — production never saw it.

Visual changes (frontend) rebuild in ~1 min; logical changes (backend) a bit more. Either way, **production is never touched until you sign off.**

## This is the new default
From now on, when you ask me to change something, I'll do it **in staging first** and give you the staging URL to review — rather than editing the live system directly like we did earlier this session. Let me lock that in so I don't forget:
